name: hover, pointer, any-pointer
plain: Whether the main input is a mouse, finger or stylus and whether hover works.
meaning: pointer is coarse for touch, fine for mouse or pen; hover is hover or none. any-* variants say if any attached device qualifies, revealing a mouse on a tablet or a touchscreen on a laptop.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can tell if you use a mouse, finger or stylus, and whether hover works
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads.
can: Check what your main input is
Check which other inputs are attached, at a rough level
cannot: See which mouse brand or model you use
Tell when you plug in a device later without checking again

story.what_it_is: Tells a page whether the main input is a mouse, finger or pen, and whether hover works.

marketing.name: pointer and hover media features
marketing.pitch: Document how a page can detect if the main input is precise like a mouse or coarse like a finger.

story.for_you: You never see the check. It is why buttons are bigger on a touch screen, and menus open on hover with a mouse but need a tap on a phone.
story.for_makers: Makers use it to give touch users larger buttons and mouse users hover tools. It is also a clue that tells phones from laptops, and helps catch fake devices.

use_cases.example: A browser game shows on screen touch controls on a phone and keyboard hints on a laptop.
A drawing app turns on pressure and pen tools when a stylus is detected.
A store shows a zoom on hover for mouse users and a tap to zoom for phone users.
A site chooses a bigger, easier to tap ad close button on touch screens.
A bot check sees a device that claims to be a phone but supports hover and a fine pointer, which is odd, and adds risk.
A site makes tap targets larger for people who use coarse input or have shaky hands.
A booking site shows hover tips about fees with a mouse and tap to expand on a phone.
